newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania seems set for vital elections.
newsitem.headline: Albania seems set for vital elections.

text.p: Albania on Thursday seemed set for elections aimed at stopping a slide back into anarchy as European envoy Franz Vranitzky said political parties have agreed to stand in the vote.
A state of lawlessness still reigns in several areas of the chaotic Balkan nation after riots and looting in March and the June 29 elections are regarded as vital to restore order.

"(Albanian) Prime Minister (Bashkim) Fino called me last night and he told me the political parties had agreed to solve the political situation in Albania...They have confirmed the election will be held on June 29," Vranitzky told a news conference in Vienna.

Most parties of Fino's National Reconciliation Government had threatened to boycott the vote, saying President Sali Berisha and his former ruling Democratic Party passed election laws designed to tilt the election in their favour.
Vranitzky, envoy for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), has been toiling since March to bring agreement and has made five fruitless trips so far.

Speaking after addressing the OSCE's Vienna-based permanent council, the former Austrian chancellor said the parties had agreed on a number of sticking points, including the makeup of a central electoral commission and regional commissions.
Fino on Wednesday sent an appeal for full "Bosnia-style" monitoring of the election to persuade parties that fair play would be assured and persuade them to stand in the vote.
Vranitzky said the OSCE would give its total support for help in preparing the election and send as many observers as necessary together the Council of Europe.
"We will help Albania. The whole international community is speaking with unanimity. There are no dissenting voices," Vranitzky added.
As Vranitzky made his announcement, the Socialist Party, the second-largest party and main rival to the Democrats, was still meeting to decide on the election.
The Socialists pulled out of the last poll in May 1996, accusing the Democrats of rigging the vote. That election was called seriously flawed by the OSCE.
"We will take part in the elections only if full guarantees are given by international institutions," Socialist chairman Fatos Nano told newspaper Gazeta Shqiptare.
One politician said Albania needed the same kind of all-embracing monitoring of its election as in Bosnia.
Last year's voting there was largely organised by outside bodies such as the OSCE, which mobilised a large force to help compile voter registers and monitor every polling station.
Other parties were not immediately available to say whether they were considering taking part.
The country is far calmer since a March uprising, when people took to the streets in fury over the collapse of pyramid investment schemes that left many of them penniless.

But killings and shootings still take place almost daily and swathes of the country remain outside government control, particularly the south, which blamed Berisha for the collapse of the schemes and saw the worst violence.
The international community has sent a barrage of warnings to Albania, saying aid and assistance which the impoverished country vitally needs may be withdrawn if they do not go ahead.
Italy, leader of a 6,000-strong multinational force that is protecting the aid supplies, has said the troops may pull out if the elections do not take place.
